reason: The court applied CPC section 114(2) and the duty to keep marked documents of record as a necessary basis for amending the partition shares.
The statement omits the material testamentary context that the administrator had a statutory discovery remedy under CPC section 712 for the withheld estate information.
The court expressly distinguished CPC section 14 from section 18 when upholding the addition of the party.
The holding was that this petitioner should be added to avoid a separate rectification action, not that every party seeking rectification must be joined.
The court held that prescription is suspended by an action only against a claimant who has been made a party, and the statement preserves that defendant limitation.
The court held that section 55 of the National Savings Bank Act validly passes title by a Bank certificate of sale notwithstanding the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance objection.
The balance-of-probability statement was made for due execution of a will and is too broad without that probate context.
The court allowed probate because it would give effect to the testator's wishes where the essential elements of execution were satisfied.
The court treated only the specific contradictions about how the will witnesses were gathered as immaterial, not contradictions generally.
The court quashed the cancellation because the State-land lease permit holder had to be given notice and a hearing before cancellation.
The natural-justice passage was an alternative observation because the court had already found an express statutory hearing procedure for lease-permit cancellation.
The rule was decided on the limited nature of the leasehold and subtenancy, not by construing Rent Act section 8.
The holding was limited to a defaulting partition party's right to object to the final scheme where the Partition Law made no prohibition.
The statement omits that the transferees bought only contingent rights pending a partition action and therefore had no interest in the corpus.
The court only held that these pending-action transferees could not be awarded undivided rights, not that courts cannot award undivided rights by judgment and interlocutory decree.
The definition of a praedial servitude was central to dismissing the claim because the plaintiff was not owner of the dominant tenement.
The court construed Prescription Ordinance section 5 in the usufructuary mortgage context and held time could run only from breach of the relevant condition.
The subordinate-entry and overt-act rule was a prescriptive-possession holding, but the cited section 5 concerns mortgage actions rather than that rule.
The bond-terms limitation on a usufructuary mortgagee was part of the holding, but it was not itself a construction of Prescription Ordinance section 5.
The obstruction-removal discussion was expressly addressed as an academic point after the appeal was already disposed of for want of reasons.
The rule omits the condition that death occurred after decree while an appeal was pending and wrongly links the point to CPC section 653 sequestration.
The court found surrender or waiver of the ande rights, not a general rule that sale of land may leave those rights unextinguished, and CPC section 147 was not the construed provision.
The attesting-witness conduct supported waiver or surrender on these facts, but the actual statutory issue was under the Agrarian Services Act rather than CPC section 147.
The inference depended materially on the tenant also signing as witness and acting as intermediary, and the cited CPC section 147 was not the provision construed.
The court held that legal title remained in Haramanis Soysa as trustee while only beneficial interest vested in the temple, defeating the plaintiff's locus standi.
